description_ru: Как мозг создаёт и хранит воспоминания: от случая пациента Г. М. до практических советов по запоминанию.
text:
Think about the last time you tried to remember a phone number, or the name of someone you had met only once. Sometimes the information appeared instantly, and sometimes it escaped, however hard you tried. Memory seems simple, but it is one of the most complex things your brain does. It involves billions of cells, several different regions and a continuous process of storing, repairing and sometimes rewriting your past. Scientists have learned a great deal about it in the last hundred years, and the story begins with a very unlucky man.

In 1953, an American patient known for decades only as H.M. (his real name was Henry Molaison) had a surgery to treat severe epilepsy. The surgeons removed parts of his brain on both sides, including a region called the hippocampus. The epilepsy improved, but the result was shocking. Henry could remember his childhood and the skills he had learned, but he could no longer create new long-term memories. He could meet someone ten times and greet them as a stranger each time. This case showed scientists that the hippocampus plays a central role in forming new memories.

To understand how this works, we need to look at the basic unit of the brain, the neuron. The human brain contains about 86 billion neurons, and each one can connect to thousands of others. When you experience something, a group of neurons becomes active together. The connections between them, called synapses, become stronger when they are used. Scientists summarise this idea in a famous phrase: "Neurons that fire together, wire together." A memory, in other words, is not a single object stored in one place. It is a pattern of connections spread across the brain.

Psychologists usually describe three types of memory. The first is sensory memory, which lasts only a second or two and holds the images and sounds around you. The second is short-term, or working, memory. It allows you to keep a few items in your mind, such as a postcode that you are about to type. In the 1950s, the psychologist George Miller suggested that most people can hold about seven items at once, although more recent studies indicate that the real number may be closer to four. The third type is long-term memory, which can last for decades and has no known limit.

How does information move from short-term to long-term memory? Attention is the first requirement. If you are checking your phone while someone tells you their name, the information never gets properly stored. The second ingredient is meaning. Facts that connect to something you already know are far easier to remember than random ones. The third, and perhaps the most surprising, is sleep. During deep sleep, the brain replays the events of the day and moves important information into long-term storage. Students who sleep well after studying often score higher on tests than those who stay up all night.

Forgetting is also normal, and it is even useful. In the 1880s, the German scientist Hermann Ebbinghaus tested himself with lists of meaningless syllables and found that most of what we learn disappears within a few days, unless we review it. His "forgetting curve" is steep at the beginning and flatter later. Without forgetting, your mind would fill up with unimportant details, such as every car you have ever passed on the road. The brain seems to keep what is repeated, emotional or useful.

That brings us to some practical advice. One of the best methods is spaced repetition, which means reviewing information at increasing intervals: after a day, then three days, then a week and so on. Testing yourself is also more effective than simply rereading, because the effort of recalling strengthens the connection. Explaining a topic to another person, or drawing a picture of it, helps too. And regular exercise has been shown to increase the volume of the hippocampus, at least in older adults.

Emotions also play a powerful part. The amygdala, a small almond-shaped structure next to the hippocampus, becomes active when something frightening or exciting happens, and it tells the hippocampus that the event is important. That is why you can remember exactly where you were during a surprising event, but not what you had for lunch last Tuesday. Strong feelings act like a highlighter pen on the page of experience.

Finally, it is worth remembering that memory is not a perfect recording. Each time you recall an event, your brain rebuilds it, and small details can change. Researchers have shown that people can sincerely remember things that never happened, if the suggestion is strong enough. This does not mean that your memory is useless. It means that it is a creative process, closer to storytelling than to filming. If you look after your brain with sleep, exercise and curiosity, it will serve you well for a lifetime.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Короткий звук между «и» и «ы»; не растягивайте его как «ии».
Задняя часть языка касается мягкого нёба, звук идёт через нос; не добавляйте «г» в конце.
В конце слога «л» твёрдое, кончик языка у дёсен, а задняя часть языка поднята.
Выделяйте ударный слог длиннее и громче, остальные слоги редуцируйте.

questions.question: What happened to Henry Molaison after his surgery?
questions.answer: He could not form new long-term memories.

questions.question: How many neurons does the human brain have?
Why is sleep important for memory?
questions.answer: The brain replays the day and moves information into long-term storage.
